---
title: "AutoResearch"
---

## Upstream design

Andrej Karpathy's AutoResearch lets a coding agent propose changes to a small language-model training script. Its documented protocol keeps data preparation and evaluation separate from the editable training script, uses a five-minute training budget per trial, and ranks candidates by validation bits per byte [@karpathy2026autoresearch]. Comparable trials still require a consistent runtime environment. Repeated selection on the validation set can favor configurations that happen to perform well on that set.

## Local experiment

The [Python lab](../labs/index.qmd#the-autoresearch-loop) models the selection loop with constant integer predictors over a fixed synthetic dataset. A scripted proposer supplies up to four candidates. The evaluator computes mean absolute error (MAE) on the same validation examples each time. The controller keeps a proposal only when it strictly improves the incumbent and charges one trial per attempt. The holdout is evaluated after selection.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-selection-loop
%%| fig-cap: "The controller compares each candidate with the current incumbent before spending the next trial."
%%| fig-alt: "A baseline enters a budget check. While trials remain, the controller proposes and scores a candidate, then keeps or discards it before returning to the budget check. On exhaustion it evaluates the winner on holdout data."
flowchart TD
    B[Score baseline] --> T{Trials remaining?}
    T -->|Yes| P[Propose candidate]
    P --> V[Measure validation MAE]
    V --> I{Strict improvement?}
    I -->|Yes| K[Update incumbent]
    I -->|No| D[Retain incumbent]
    K --> T
    D --> T
    T -->|No| H[Score winner on holdout]
```

```{dot}
//| file: ../assets/diagrams/autoresearch-boundaries.dot

//| fig-alt: "The controller reads candidates from the scripted proposer and requests scores from the evaluator. The evaluator reads validation data and reads holdout data at the end. The controller writes trial decisions to the report."
```

## Reproduce the example

```bash
python -m labs.autoresearch --budget 4
```

The baseline predicts 0 and has validation MAE 3. The four proposals are 2, 1, 3, and 4. The controller accepts 2 and 3. The final predictor is 3, with validation MAE 0.5 and holdout MAE 1.0. This run illustrates selection under a budget. Its four-point holdout is too small to support a claim about generalization.

## Building AutoResearch block by block {#building-autoresearch-block-by-block}

The course builds AutoResearch incrementally. Each block answers one design question and adds one piece to the system. By Block 14 the pieces form an agent for machine-learning modeling work with validated tool calls, isolated sub-agents for each role, a durable experiment ledger, recovery from failures, a protected evaluator and holdout, and evaluation evidence that justifies deploying it. Rows for blocks that have not yet been developed describe the plan.

| Block | Piece added to AutoResearch | Design question |
|---|------|----|
| 01 | Protocol and ownership map: a fixed evaluator, a promotion rule, compute and trial limits, and a holdout scored once on the frozen selection. The policy proposes trials or a stop, and the runtime authorizes, runs, scores, promotes, records, and stops | Who chooses the next experiment, and what does the runtime enforce? |
| 02 | Explicit controller: modes, a transition table, checkpoints, and reconciliation of ambiguous outcomes | Which transitions must be explicit, and what does a checkpoint prove? |
| 03 | Typed tools to edit training code in a sandbox and to submit, score, look up, and promote trials, with validation, authorization, and operation IDs. No tool can write to the evaluator or the data | How does a proposal become a validated operation? |
| 04 | Durable experiment ledger and context builder | What enters the policy's context, and what must survive a restart? |
| 05 | Research planner that revises hypotheses when the evidence warrants it | When should the plan change? |
| 06 | Architecture choice for the workload, such as planner–executor or supervisor–worker, justified against a single controller | Who should own the next decision and the state needed to make it? |
| 07 | Isolated sub-agents for proposing, running, and reviewing, each with scoped permissions. Scoring stays with the fixed evaluator, which no sub-agent can modify | When do separate roles earn their coordination cost? |
| 08 | Tools exposed through MCP, and the choice between exposing a sub-agent as a tool or through an agent-to-agent protocol | Which boundary should be standardized? |
| 09 | Evaluation harness against a fixed batch and a conventional optimizer at matched budgets, with validation-overfitting checks such as fresh-seed re-scoring of the final incumbent | Does learned selection beat strong baselines? |
| 10 | Retries, idempotent writes, and recovery from crashes and ambiguous failures | How does the run resume accurately after a failure? |
| 11 | Runs that span hours or days, with resume and replanning | How does a run continue hours later? |
| 12 | Queues, GPU scheduling, tracing, and cost controls across many runs | What must the runtime guarantee at scale? |
| 13 | A proposal policy improved from logged runs. Training data comes from validation-era logs, and holdout results never enter it | Did training improve the policy that drives the agent? |
| 14 | Complete design review and deployment evidence | What evidence justifies deploying the added autonomy? |

The [design exercises](../exercises/index.qmd) combine several pieces, such as an experiment service with approvals.
